unit.title: Computational thinking, unplugged and with blocks

video.title: Break it down: Four ways computer scientists think
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Guess my number, I told my class: from one to a hundred. Half of them guessed one, two, three, four, and gave up. One girl said fifty, then twenty-five, and found it in six guesses.
Today: breaking problems down, and the four ways computer scientists think.

Computational thinking is a way of solving problems that computers made famous. It has four parts. Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms. You and your pupils use them already; naming them helps you teach them.

Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller ones. Planning a school sports day is too big to do at once. Break it into the races, the timetable, the equipment and the prizes. Each small part is easy to solve on its own.

Pattern recognition means spotting what is the same, like the loops in the robot’s program. Abstraction means keeping only what matters. A bus map leaves out the shops and trees, and keeps the stops. It’s simpler, and more useful.

You can find these four in every subject. In maths, decompose a long word problem. In science, spot the pattern in a week of temperatures. In language, a summary is an abstraction. In PE, the rules of a game are an algorithm.
Quick check! A pupil draws a map of the way to school with only the turns and the landmarks, nothing else. Which part of computational thinking is that?
Abstraction. The map leaves out the houses and the colours, and keeps what you need to find your way. Good abstractions are everywhere: a timetable, a register, a recipe card.

Back to guess my number. Both ways are algorithms, and both find the number. One by one can take a hundred guesses. Halving the range each time never needs more than seven. Same job, very different work.

Play it in class. One pupil thinks of a number; the class guesses, and hears only higher or lower. Count the guesses for each strategy on the board. Pupils discover halving for themselves, and that’s the best way to learn an algorithm.
In the app, open Guess the number. With one to a hundred, press only Try the middle: you never need more than seven guesses. Then race one by one against halving, with numbers up to a thousand.
Your turn. Which of these is decomposition: splitting a class play into scenes, costumes and music, or drawing a seating plan with only names?

Splitting the play. Remember the four parts: decomposition breaks it down, patterns spot what repeats, abstraction keeps what matters, and algorithms give the steps. And some algorithms do the same job with far less work.
Try it in class tomorrow: play Guess my number. Count the guesses for one by one and for halving, write both on the board, and ask: why does halving win? Then name the four parts in today’s lesson.

checkpoints.prompt: A map of the way to school with only the turns and landmarks. Which part is it?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — keeping only what matters and leaving out the rest is abstraction.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — leaving out details and keeping what matters is abstraction.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — breaking a big job into smaller parts is decomposition.
